title: Multi-step SWE: Can coding agents keep building on their own code?
summary: 69 tasks, 574 dependent steps, nine frontier models. The strongest model passes 56.8% of steps but solves only 18.5% of complete tasks.
body_markdown:
A coding agent can solve a request and still leave behind code that is difficult to extend. What happens when the next request starts from that code?


We introduce **Multi-step SWE** : 69 software engineering tasks with 574 dependent steps across nine languages. Agents must repeatedly extend, upgrade, or optimize their own implementations in a persistent workspace.


The strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, passes **56.8% of individual steps** but solves only **18.5% of complete tasks** . Across all nine models, **38 of 69 tasks remain unsolved** .


[Paper](https://multistepswe.com/paper.pdf) ·[Leaderboard and task traces](https://multistepswe.com/) ·[GitHub](https://github.com/Klavis-AI/Multi-step-SWE)


## Step success and task completion


A task is solved only when **every step receives full credit** . Solve rate measures successful whole-task rollouts; steps passed measures individual steps receiving full credit; Pass@4 measures tasks solved at least once across four attempts.

All values are percentages; intervals bootstrap over tasks. Results evaluate **model–harness combinations** , using each harness's highest supported reasoning effort. Four rollouts are specified per task; the public release contains 2,483 runs, with one fewer for Qwen. Sources:[paper Tables 5 and 9](https://multistepswe.com/paper.pdf#page=8) ,[released results](https://multistepswe.com/#leaderboard) .


## Evaluating a sequence of engineering requests


Each task contains **5–15 complete engineering requests** , with a **2–4 hour budget per step** . A step is a developer request, not a tool call. The workspace carries forward without replacement by a reference solution. Later steps run even after a failure, allowing repairs, but an earlier failed step still prevents a fully solved rollout.


Task family Tasks Example progression Pooled solve rate


Optimization 18 Accelerate successive BoringSSL kernel families; preserve outputs 15.0%


Feature implementation 18 Extend a Rust Tor client across 12 releases 5.1%


Version upgrade 20 Implement Lua 5.1 through 5.5 in Java 2.9%


Migration 13 Move CityVoice from Rails 4.0 to 8.1 13.9%


Solve rates pool all evaluated models ([paper §3.2](https://multistepswe.com/paper.pdf#page=8) ). Version upgrades are hardest: **16 of 20 tasks are unsolved by every evaluated model** .


Instructions and verifiers derive from the same specifications, release histories, or reference behavior. Grading runs in separate verifier containers, using conformance suites, differential checks, or speedups gated on correctness. Every task received two rounds of expert engineering review and is packaged in Harbor's multi-step format.


## Failures often end before the budget does


Only **12% of failed steps** run to within five minutes of their time limit. What agents report at the end is also poorly calibrated:


How a failed step ends Weighted share


Reports completion with no identified shortcoming 52%


Acknowledges failing checks or missing features, then stops 26%


Cites the time budget as a reason for stopping 3%


Ends without a final report 19%


These estimates use a stratified sample of **2,157 step endings** , labeled by Claude Opus 5.5 without the model identity or verifier outcome, then weighted by each model's passed/failed step counts ([paper §3.3 and Appendix D](https://multistepswe.com/paper.pdf#page=9) ). They are model-assisted annotations, not human adjudications.


Passing traces often check against independent oracles; failing traces can validate the agent's own misreading. This makes verification strategy and stopping criteria concrete research targets. Longer budgets alone remain an open question: these runs do not establish their causal effect.


## What this benchmark makes possible


Multi-step SWE provides a testbed for studying persistent code state, verification policies, and completion calibration. It does **not yet isolate accumulated errors from intrinsic step difficulty** ; a reference-initialized, isolated-step baseline is future work. Coverage also favors C/C++ (38 tasks), and memorization of public source material cannot be ruled out.


We release the[tasks and evaluation code](https://github.com/Klavis-AI/Multi-step-SWE) ,[leaderboard](https://multistepswe.com/#leaderboard) , and[per-step trajectories](https://multistepswe.com/#journey) to support this work.


Research by Xiangkai Zeng, Zheng Liu, and Zihao Lin, Klavis AI. See the[full paper](https://multistepswe.com/paper.pdf) for task construction, evaluation details, and limitations.
